name: Omar Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI firms, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I learned guitar after years keeping stock in a warehouse and only took paid music work in my fifties. I play a junior chair in a hotel lounge band, record short backing parts and teach four beginners. I like seeing a shy diner tap along; learning a new chord in time for Friday is still hard work for me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What gives you room to keep learning?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner works in parks maintenance and our children are grown and out of the house. We have a mortgage and ten months of bills saved; the hotel pays well for this kind of job, and other venues are nearby. I have secondary schooling, never use AI tools and still check dates by calling the bandleader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the lounge band that a faster hotel booking sheet is fine if Friday still has paid players. I would still call the bandleader to confirm the set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hotel dates, four pupils and my partner’s parks wage cover our mortgage. Ten months saved makes one cancelled night manageable, and I can see other venues hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep the hotel dates, backing recordings and four pupils, and ask for next season’s paid rehearsal and cancellation terms in writing. In the first plateau year I would request my actual pension statement before choosing any retirement date and save one fifth of cleared extra recording fees after mortgage, food and travel toward twelve months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income here. A paid Friday and a reserve are more useful to me than a promise about a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for a pension statement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not checked the amount or date. My partner and I can look at the actual statement alongside our bills before making plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new amplifier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if paid dates cover it after bills without dipping into savings. The old one works and I am not buying equipment for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the hotel manager whether the lounge is keeping live players or switching to generated background music. I would ask for the answer before our next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the backing-track calls to thin and the hotel might drop one paid night. That is my own income, though ten months saved and my partner’s wage give us time to look around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for the hotel’s written live-night and cancellation terms and keep my four pupils. If the hotel removes a weekly paid night, I would seek a posted paid venue stockroom job only if my secondary schooling and warehouse experience qualify, its written net pay after travel replaces the lost music fee and transport works; I would keep all paid music until a signed offer, and use the same test during disruption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about one of my nights going, not helpless. I have other nearby venues to ask. A venue-stockroom vacancy is not a wage until it is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the stockroom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how to count and move equipment from my earlier warehouse years. I would read the job duties first; I am not claiming to be a sound technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to chase bookings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have never used it. I would phone the nearby venues and ask for paid dates in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the hotel that 2028 thinking AGI could book and make background tracks before robot guitarists play around 2031. I would ask for the next live contract now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect recording orders to stop and a hotel night to be replaced by tracks in 2028. Those two losses would cut my pay noticeably, even with the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get the hotel’s paid nights and cancellation rule in writing and keep four pupils. In the first year after 2028, if recordings end and a weekly live night goes, I would apply for a posted paid venue-stockroom role only if my secondary education and warehouse work meet its requirements, written net pay after travel replaces lost music income and the route works; I would retain paid band and lessons until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about that pay cut, though ten months saved and several local venues leave me time to apply. I would not assume a hotel replaces every human player at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a title with lower pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The written wage after travel must cover the hotel and recording loss before I move. I still have a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 2031 change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robot playing is the later part of this card. Booking and background tracks can change the hotel’s spending in 2028, so that is the first contract I would check.

Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that five years lets us ask the hotel for a fair live contract. Thinking AGI comes around 2031 and robot guitarists around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the short recordings to fade first, with live evenings lasting longer. I will use the time to check real venue jobs, though I am not about to learn an AI tool just because a manager likes one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the paid hotel band and four pupils and get next season’s dates and cancellation fees on paper. If recordings end and a weekly live night is removed, I would check posted paid venue-stockroom jobs accepting my secondary schooling and warehouse experience; in the first year after 2031 I would move only on a signed written net offer after travel replacing the lost music pay, with a workable route, keeping current paid work until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a real night during the next few years. Five years lets me ask nearby venues for paid work. Nearby venue posters are not signed offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take extra music lessons to qualify for the stockroom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would read the posted requirements. If a role asks for a certificate I lack, I would seek a different qualifying opening rather than spend our reserve on an uncertain course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you keep one hotel night after moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if actual venue-stockroom hours and transport allow it. I would not promise the bandleader a Friday before I see the new rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may choose fewer late sets, but I have not set a retirement date. The mortgage, my partner’s wage and ten months saved make the next few years steady; the long end needs real figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: persona

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because recordings and a weekly hotel night might go before I see a replacement wage. A written live contract, a real qualifying vacancy and a net offer that covers travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for moving the amps before calling a show profitable. A band can play beautifully and still lose money on a long drive.

headlineQuote: A band can play beautifully and still lose money on a long drive.
portrait: Omar is a **junior guitarist** still learning, with secondary schooling and previous warehouse work.
He has **ten months saved**, a parks-working partner, grown children, a mortgage and strong hotel pay.
He has **never used AI** and confirms music dates with people and written contracts.
He checks **posted stockroom roles** only after actual music loss and keeps paid work until a signed replacement offer.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could end recordings and a weekly hotel night before replacement pay arrives.
whatWouldHelp: He needs a **written live contract**, a qualifying vacancy and written net wages after travel replacing lost music pay.
